Before you splurge on a bunch of gardening supplies, you may want to think about what you want to grow. Knowing what you want to grow may affect your choice of planting material.

I live in Hong Kong and have a small garden on my balcony as well. I have chosen clay pots for my balcony as the sun can get very strong, to the point where it started to affect some plastic containers that I had. Good luck with your garden.

Yah, happy planting.

But I might suggest holding off on the the crystals and buy different types of soil instead and create various mixes. You can combine things like compost, potting soil, clay, gravel and sand to simulate different soil types that hold water in different ways. You can make small jars of each to test and learn.

A couple of comments....

The tubs are a good choice. To keep the sides from bowing out, it's better to leave the top on and cut holes in it .

Plastic planter boxes would be a much better choice than mason jars.

Good drainage is an absolute must in any container garden. It's especially important early when its cool and there aren't a lot of plants and heat drawing water out fast enough to prevent rotting roots. On the other hand, with two tomatoes in a tub, by mid summer they'll fill the box completely with roots and water will be drawn out so fast you'll be watering way more than you expect. When it gets warm, you'll want a tray to hold water to give the soil some time to absorb it. I use dollar store dish pans under 5 gallon sized bucket pots.

I got a couple cheap led spotlights (box type, not round reflectors) to replace the shop lights I use for sprouting. They are great and would be useful for other applications if plant lighting becomes less important. In my experience, adding additional light is worthwhile. Most led spotlights don't come wired so make sure you're prepared for that. Many reviews say the cheap ones have a high failure rate though. From what I've read, you want daylight white bulbs if possible...cool white ok but avoid the warm white. (I actually bought a warm white to do some tests to see if it makes a big difference.)

I'm interested in your arduino and android plans. I've got some arduino nano's I've done a bit with and I need a simple project to motivate me to move forward with them. I've done some work (incomplete but useful) on using them for remote sensors.

For a cheap soil mix, I use a bale of compressed peat mix with two bags of play sand and a couple scoops of powdered limestone and some composted cow manure. The sand helps water flow through the peat both for drainage and to help it re-wet quickly.

My parents grew tons on their balcony...lucky for them it faced full south, but they used a lot of different containers and had a ton of success. Ideas....buckets are great for potatoes. Not sure if you'll get enough sun, but one of those tubs or a separate 5 gallon pail might let you get a nice harvest of small new potatoes. Also...remember up you,can also go for height with trellises or even just strings. Peas, beans or, in my dads case, morning glories can be train up some twine or jute. Radishes and young lettuces also work well.

Note: This course was made using Unity 5.2. Any version of Unity 5 is compatible with this course. Also, all scripting is 100% done from scratch.

What is the course about?

This course is all about learning game development using the Unity3D Game Engine. We will be covering topics that go all the way from installing the engine, to making a character move in world, to creating very simple AI.

C# experience is recommended, but not required as I explain absolutely everything about what I'm doing and why I'm doing it. Although this course is mostly programming, I also take the time to go through the interface, set up basic animations in Mecanim (Unity's animation system), and use most of the commonly used windows within the interface.

There are always multiple ways to do things in game development. Because I want you to keep an open mind as to the possibilities Unity brings you, when I'm doing something that may feel repetitive, I always go about it a different way. This way you will end up getting more familiar with the engine.

Although this course is the perfect foundation to start as a Unity Developer, all learning levels should benefit from this course one way or another because of the different ways in which I approach situations. That being said, this course is meant for beginner level students.

What's included in the course?

  • 30 Lectures, 29 videos and 6 hours of content
  • All art/sound assets
  • The finalized version of the Unity Project we are going to be creating

How is the course structured?

This course is divided into 3 sections.

The first section is all about learning your way through the engine. In this section, I show you where to go to install the engine, go through the commonly used windows in the interface, and talk about terminology Unity Developers use on a day-to-day basis.

The second section is about creating the player's and all the enemies' behaviors in game. There are a total of 3 enemies (robots, laser fences, and security cameras).

The third section is about finalizing the environment by adding sounds and a few other things that bring the environment to life. In this section, we'll also be making a build of the application for use by the end user.

What should you expect by the end of the course?

By the end of the course, you will be armed with the knowledge necessary to feel confident/comfortable when using the engine for your own projects. Learning new things within the engine should be very easy at this point.

If you have any questions or concerns, feel free to contact me and I'll be happy to reply as soon as possible.
